title: The Fragile Confidence Loop in Learning
author: Debbie Thompson
summary: Thompson, who taught in English secondary schools for more than twenty four years, names a pattern she calls the fragile confidence loop: a teacher praises a student as smart, the label becomes part of the student's identity, and thereafter any task that might disprove the label registers as a threat, so the student stops asking questions, stops answering them, and chooses the safest possible route through the work. She traces her own reversal on this, having been trained to praise generously and then noticing that anxious and introverted students squirmed or froze when singled out as smart, a reaction her departmental colleagues confirmed from their own conversations with students. The extended case is Terry, a fourteen year old labelled bright for years whose confidence collapsed after one poor result on quadratic equations, and whose self talk shifted to not wanting to get it wrong and having once been good at maths. Thompson's diagnosis is that Terry's identity was built on speed and instant understanding, so needing effort read to her as failure. She then situates the problem in Carol Dweck's work, with the important caveat that growth mindset is not something a teacher can instruct a student to adopt but a condition teachers create by making struggle safe and mistakes ordinary. Her practical alternative is process anchored affirmation, replacing trait praise with comments on persistence, pattern noticing, and strategy change, and she lists five classroom practices that aim at confidence a student can generate internally rather than receive.
points: The mechanism she identifies is identity protection: once smart becomes who a student is, difficulty threatens the self rather than the task.
She warns the resulting withdrawal is easily misread by later teachers as laziness or work avoidance rather than fear of exposure.
Her reading of Dweck insists growth mindset cannot be told to students, only cultivated through conditions where struggle feels safe and effort feels meaningful.
She offers specific replacement language, praising sticking with a step, noticing a pattern, or changing strategy, instead of naming a trait.
Even wrong answers get named for the thinking they contain, such as noticing a mismatch or checking an idea, so error becomes usable rather than shameful.
quotes: Sometimes in those lesson I noticed that a student would answer a question correctly but was nervous when they were giving their answer. The teacher usually responded enthusiastically and said: “You’re so smart!”.
Those students often felt that they couldn’t take risks with their learning later on, as being wrong meant that they were no longer smart, and so it was safer for them to stay quiet in class.

The fragile confidence loop can start with a teacher labelling a student with a trait, like being smart, and then that trait becomes part of their identity over time. So any challenge that risks showing that the trait is wrong can feel dangerous to a student, and they avoid challenges to protect their identity.

And later on I realised that students sometimes carry the result of this into classes. It’s invisible and could be misread as laziness or avoidance of work. Underneath there might be a fear of being exposed as not smart.
Her identity had been built on being quick, and on being someone who understood new topics almost instantly. So when a topic required more effort, she interpreted that effort as failure.
A student develops a growth mindset because teachers create the conditions in which struggle feels safe, mistakes feel normal, and effort feels meaningful.
So instead of praising traits, I say things like: “I like how you stuck with that step.”, or “You noticed the pattern, that’s great thinking.”, or “You changed strategy when it got tricky.
Confidence that comes from within is the only kind that lasts over time.
